full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam, J: Both the civil petitions for leave to appeal are directed against the Judgment and Order dated 12-4-2017 passed by High Court Division in First Appeal No. 508 of 1999 (heard analogously with First Appeal No.121 of 2021) modifying the judgment and decree dated 25-3-1999 passed by the Sub Ordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 200 of 1993 decreeing the suit. 

 3. The defendants contested the suit by filing separate written statements. The defendant No.1 in the written statement stated that the suit property belonged to him as well as his minor sons and the defendant only executed the deed of sale so far as it relates to 2.50 khatas i.e half of the property in question and since the plaintiffs failed to perform their part as per the terms and condition of the deed of agreement for sale the plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree for Specific Performance of Contract. 

 6. The trial court after hearing the parties and considering the facts and circumstances, materials on record and the provision of law decreed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract. 

 7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the Judgment of the trial court the defendant No.1 and defendant Nos. 2-3 filed two separate First Appeal being No. 508 of 1999 and First Appeal No. 121 of 2001 before the High Court Division which was heard analogously and by a single judgment the High Court Division, dismissed the same and modified the judgment and decree of the trial court. Hence the instant Civil petition for leave to appeal. 

 8. Mr Md Nurul Amin, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner in Civil Petition for leave to appeal No. 1061 of 2018 submits that the court below without applying its judicial mind and without considering the facts and circumstances and other materials on record most illegally and in an arbitrary manner decreed the suit and thereby committed error which requires interference by this court. 

 "In lagesh Chandra Das vs Farida Hasan 1983 BLD (AD) 22.5 this Court refused to enforce the contract on the ground of hardship when two circumstances were established (a) a very low price (b) contract was performed under compelling circumstances when the members of the minority community were contemplating to migrate from the country In a similar situation a Division Bench of Karnataka High Court considered the problem in Ranganayakamma vs Govinda Narayan AIR 1982 (ant) 264. The facts are exactly on all fours with the present case. There also her husband made a contract for selling his dwelling house and soon thereafter he died, the plaintiff brought the suit for specific performance in 1970. The consideration was Taka 21,000 and advance was paid Taka 3,000. Since the deed of sale was not executed the suit was filed. The defence was mainly on hardship. The Division Bench carefully considered the defence and concluded If we decree the suit, she will be deprived of that income too, for the rest of her life with no shelter to cover her head, There can, therefore, be no justification for us to tell her that she should sell the house and go on pilgrimage never to return," The Court considered that the plaintiff was a businessman in that case and not a helpless widow like the defendant. In view of those facts, the Court refused to enforce the specific performance no doubt, but appreciated the gesture of the appellant to return the advance amount by three limes. This case shows the judicial anxiety to do justice when faced with the similar situation as emphasised in item-II namely, hardship vs hardship qualified by legal mandate "hardship which he did not foresee vis-a-vis "no such hardship would accrue to the plaintiff." Having given our anxious consideration to the facts of this case, we are of the opinion that this contract should, not be enforced specifically if the defendant appellants return the entire advance money of Taka 8,500 with a solatiurn of Taka 1,00,000 to the plaintiff respondent. In Jagesh Chandra Das's case (Supra) we directed the return of Taka 300paid as advance and compensation of Taka 40,000 to the plaintiff failing which "the plaintiffs suit stands decreed in full." Mr BN Chowdhury, learned Counsel, appearing for the defendant-appellants, in his characteristic manner informed the Court that his client will be bound by any reasonable solatium if pronouncement is made by the Court." 

 "Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act states that granting of a decree for specific performance of contract is a discretion of the court and the same must be exercised not arbitrarily but on the basis of sound and reasonable principles and capable of correction by a Court of appeal. Illustration of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act speaks that the Court may not exercise the discretion for specific performance of contract where the performance would involve some hardship on the part of the defendant which he did not foresee whereas its non-performance would involve no such hardship on the plaintiff. It was specifically argued before the High Court Division that the Subordinate Judge ought to have dismissed the suit on the ground of hardship of the defendant. It appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division considered the question of hardship in extenso and found that the defendant Md Taheruddin Mir entered into a contract with the plaintiff knowing full well that he has only one house at Kishoreganj Town and consequently, the question of hardship of the defendant was rejected by the learned Judges of the High Court Division. The question of hardship is primarily a question of fact and in the present case the learned Judges after proper exercise of their discretion rejected the contention of the defendant and upheld the decree of the trial Court." 

 19. On perusal of the evidences and exhibits it transpires that the plaintiffs have spent a substantial amount as construction costs but the benefit was enjoyed by the defendants and at the same time it also appears that the defendants also invested some money for further construction. It appears that the claim of hardships could not be raised by both the parties and at the same time if by operation of law the judgment and decree passed by the Court below is maintained nothing would be left for defendant vendor. 

 Therefore, both the leave petitions are disposed of. The Judgment and decrees passed by the Courts below are hereby set-aside. The suit is dismissed. The defendant-petitioners are directed to pay solatium of Taka 50,00,000 (fifty lac) to the plaintiff-respondent along with the amount treated by him of a sum of Taka 4,52,84954 (four lac fifty two thousand eight hundred forty nine and fifty four paisa) within 6(six) months from date in default both these petitions shall be treated as dismissed. After payment being made in the manner as stated through a pay order to the respondent No. 1, the possession of the flat which was earlier handed over to the plaintiff-respondent should be returned to the defendants.
